drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main problem: hives, swelling, a food or drug reaction, a bee sting, trouble breathing after an exposure, or something else?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main allergic complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: When did this start, and how fast did it come on after the exposure?
questions.rationale: Minutes-to-onset after exposure supports anaphylaxis.

questions.text: What were you eating, taking, stung by, or exposed to just before this started?
questions.rationale: Identifying the trigger is the key to prevention and acute care.

questions.text: Do you have itchy hives or welts that move around?
questions.rationale: Urticaria is the most common allergic skin finding.

questions.text: Is your face, lips, tongue, or throat swelling?
questions.rationale: Angioedema can threaten the airway.

questions.text: Are you wheezing, short of breath, or is your throat closing?
questions.rationale: Respiratory involvement defines anaphylaxis and needs immediate treatment.

questions.text: Have you felt faint, dizzy, nauseated, or vomited with this reaction?
questions.rationale: Cardiovascular and gut features also count toward anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Have you used an epinephrine injector, and did the symptoms come back after it wore off?
questions.rationale: Biphasic anaphylaxis can recur after initial improvement.

questions.text: What allergies do you already know about, and how severe have past reactions been?
questions.rationale: Prior anaphylaxis is the strongest predictor of another severe reaction.

questions.text: Did this start after a new medicine, antibiotic, NSAID, or contrast dye?
questions.rationale: Drugs are a leading cause of anaphylaxis and severe cutaneous reactions.

questions.text: Did this follow peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, egg, or another food?
questions.rationale: IgE food allergy is a common anaphylaxis trigger.

questions.text: Were you stung by a bee, wasp, or ant?
questions.rationale: Venom anaphylaxis needs counseling and often immunotherapy referral.

questions.text: Does this happen with latex, or after exercise, especially after certain foods?
questions.rationale: Latex and food-dependent exercise anaphylaxis are easy to miss.

questions.text: Do you take an ACE inhibitor or sitagliptin, especially if the swelling is of the tongue without hives?
questions.rationale: ACE-inhibitor angioedema often lacks hives and can recur.

questions.text: If this is hives, have they lasted more than six weeks, and do they come daily?
questions.rationale: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is managed differently from anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Do you have asthma, and is it flaring with this reaction?
questions.rationale: Asthma increases the risk of fatal anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Any blistering, peeling skin, or sores in the mouth, eyes, or genitals after a new drug?
questions.rationale: SJS/TEN is a drug emergency distinct from simple allergy.

questions.text: Any fever, joint pain, or rash a week or more after a drug or injection?
questions.rationale: Delayed drug reactions include serum sickness and DRESS.

questions.text: Do you get unusual or repeated infections, or have you been told you have an immune deficiency?
questions.rationale: Recurrent infections may indicate immunodeficiency rather than allergy.

questions.text: Are symptoms triggered by pollen, dust, cats, or mold, with sneezing and itchy eyes?
questions.rationale: Allergic rhinitis is common and usually not anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Besides the suspected trigger, what medicines and supplements do you take?
questions.rationale: Beta blockers and ACE inhibitors change anaphylaxis management.

questions.text: Do you carry epinephrine, and do you have an allergy action plan?
questions.rationale: Access to epinephrine is a core safety question after a reaction.

questions.text: Are symptoms still getting worse right now?
questions.rationale: Progressive symptoms require emergency treatment rather than more history.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Swelling of tongue or throat or trouble breathing
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report lip, tongue, or throat swelling, wheeze, or trouble breathing after an exposure?

red_flags.label: Allergic reaction with faintness or vomiting
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report an allergic reaction with dizziness, fainting, or vomiting?

red_flags.label: Facial or tongue swelling
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report swelling of the face, lips, or tongue?

red_flags.label: Blistering drug reaction with mucosal sores
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report blistering or peeling skin with mouth, eye, or genital sores after a new medicine?

red_flags.label: Reaction beginning within minutes of a trigger
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe a reaction that started within minutes of a food, sting, or medicine?

red_flags.label: Symptoms still worsening
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient say the allergic symptoms are still getting worse right now?
